_metadata.scope: Ancestor (above-item) levels of Durandus, Commentarius in libros Sententiarum (Redactio C), built from item-level interpretation.json files. Currently covers Liber 1 Prologus, Liber 1 Distinctio 37 (with its two partes), Liber 2 Distinctio 44, and partial entries for Liber 1, Liber 2, and the whole work.

jsnvu6-d1e83.summary: Durandus's Prologue to Book I, a sustained inquiry into the nature of theology, preceded by a literal division of Peter Lombard's own prologue (read through the rhetorical exordium and the four causes of a book). Its foundational move (Q1) distinguishes three senses of theology: assent to Scripture as taught, which is simply faith; the acquired habit defending and declaring the faith from better-known principles (Augustine's scientia, Lombard's project); and the habit of conclusions deduced from the articles. On the formal cause, Durandus argues that theology in none of these senses is a science properly so called: faith and science can concur in one assent about demonstrable revealed truths, but the articles themselves, their possibility, and the solution of all objections cannot be demonstrated to a wayfarer, and conclusions from inevident principles are never properly scientific (Q1). He rejects any special intermediate light between faith and glory (Q2) and any perfect abstractive knowledge of the Trinity communicable in via, since abstractive knowledge presupposes an intuition that would be beatific (Q3). Theology is not one science but several habits distinguished by object and, more formally, by middle (Q4). On the material cause, the subject of theology as Scripture is the meritorious act ordered to beatitude, while the subject of defensive theology is God under the ratio of Saviour—not God absolutely, since what is demonstrable of God belongs to metaphysics (Q5). On the final cause, scriptural theology is practical and defensive theology speculative; neither is named from heavenly contemplation, and calling theology affective does not exclude its practicality (Q6). Finally, comparing theology to other sciences, Durandus denies that it is subalternated to the science of the blessed (Q7) or to metaphysics, or that it subalternates human sciences, since proper subalternation requires the higher science to give the propter quid of the lower's principles (Q8). The Prologue thus presents a deflationary, Scripture-centred and practice-oriented account of theology as a cluster of habits, scientific only in a broad sense.
claims: Theology has three senses—assent to Scripture (identical with faith), defensive/declarative theology, and deductive theology—and is a plurality of habits, not one science
Theology in none of its senses is a science properly so called, because the articles of faith are neither self-evident nor demonstrable to wayfarers
No special light or abstractive cognition available in via makes the articles evident
The subject of scriptural theology is the meritorious act; the subject of defensive theology is God under the ratio of Saviour
Scriptural theology is practical and defensive theology speculative
Theology is neither subalternated to the science of the blessed or to metaphysics nor subalternates the human sciences

jsnvu6-d1e1800.summary: Part 1 of Distinction 37 treats how God is in things. A textual division of Lombard frames the topic: God is in all things by essence, power, and presence, in the saints by grace, and in Christ by union, with indwelling preserving divine simplicity and the distinction of persons. Question 1 argues that God is in all things as their immediate, continually operating conserving cause, his 'in-ness' constituted by order and real coexistence rather than contact, and grounds the triad of essence, presence, and power in creation and conservation, adding the graced modes of hypostatic union and adoption. Question 2 asks whether God is everywhere: in himself he is contained by no place, but he fills every place by his effects (repletive presence), a presence that begins with creation, unlike the circumscriptive presence of bodies or the definitive presence of spirits.
claims: God is present in all things as their immediate conserving cause, by essence, presence, and power
Divine presence is constituted by order and real coexistence, not by spatial contact
God is everywhere repletively, filling every place with his effects while contained by none
Beyond natural presence, God is in creatures by grace of adoption and by hypostatic union

jsnvu6-d1e1816.summary: Part 2 of Distinction 37 turns from God's presence to the location and motion of angels. A textual division of Lombard contrasts bodies (circumscribed by place and moved in place and time) with spirits (defined by place and moved only in time) and denies any local mode to God, who begins and ceases to be present in creatures without change. Question 3 rejects circumscriptive presence, definitive presence grounded in the angel's finite essence, and mere causal presence as mover, arguing instead that an angel's essence is nowhere as to situs but present 'by order' to every body it can move, a real presence prior to operation, with its apparent location being the manifestation of this presence through operation; the separated soul is placed only by divine assignment. Question 4 applies this: angels cannot be moved locally in any subject-inherent sense, and their 'motion' is either the motion of the bodies they move or the discrete succession of their operations across places, which cannot be instantaneous and need not traverse intermediates.
claims: Spiritual creatures are defined, not circumscribed, by place, while God is neither
An angel is present to bodies by order, a real but non-spatial presence, not by situs or essential limitation
An angel's apparent location is the manifestation of its order-presence through operation
Angels are not moved locally as subjects; their 'motion' is the succession of their operations or the motion of bodies they move

jsnvu6-d1e1799.summary: Distinction 37 of Book I treats presence in place, first of God and then of angels, unified by a contrast between presence by order (real, immediate coexistence grounded in causality) and presence by situs (spatial containment). Part 1 argues that God is in all things as their immediate conserving cause—by essence, presence, and power, and further by grace and hypostatic union—and is everywhere repletively, filling every place with his effects while contained by none. Part 2 applies the notion of order to angels: neither circumscribed nor located by their finite essence, angels are present by order to every body they can move, their apparent location being the manifestation of that presence in operation, so that angelic 'motion' is the discrete succession of their operations or the motion of bodies they move rather than local motion of the angel itself.
claims: God is present in all creatures as their immediate conserving cause, by essence, presence, and power, and everywhere by repletion
Presence by order, not by spatial situs, explains both divine and angelic presence
Angels are present by order to bodies they can move and are not locally moved as subjects

jsnvu6-f1e44a9.summary: Distinction 44 of Book II, the last of the book, treats power and obedience. The textual division sets out Lombard's teaching that all power, even the devil's and the power to sin, is from God and just, that obedience is not owed to power commanding against God, and that the higher authority prevails in conflicts, before turning to Book III. Question 1 argues that the power to sin, including its defectibility, is from God as first cause, rejecting the view that defectibility stems from the creature's 'being from nothing' independently of God, while denying that God is immediate cause of the evil act's deformity. Question 2 holds that prelacy, as required by right reason and the natural order, is from God, though its wrongful acquisition and use are not; in innocence, directive rule would have existed but not servile domination or coercive correction. Question 3 binds Christians in conscience to obey secular princes, believing or unbelieving, within their legitimate scope: an unbeliever's prior dominion over a convert is not dissolved by baptism but may be removed by the Church if he opposes the faith, while new dominion of unbelievers over believers is forbidden. Question 4 limits religious obedience to the rule and legitimate statutes vowed, and Question 5 ranks papal over episcopal and abbatial authority while holding that a papal command from mere will, without ecclesial necessity and against a monk's profession, exceeds papal power and need not be obeyed; only God is owed unqualified obedience.
claims: All power, including the power to sin and its defectibility, derives from God
Prelacy is from God as instituted by right reason, though not its abuse; servile domination arose only after sin
Christians owe conscientious obedience to secular rulers, believing or not, within their legitimate scope
Religious obedience is measured by the vow and the rule, not by a superior's unlimited will
The pope is owed greater obedience than bishop or abbot, but not in commands issued from mere will against the Church's utility and a monk's profession; only God is owed unqualified obedience
concepts: prelacy and the state of innocence

jsnvu6-d1e78.summary: Partial summary of Book I, resting only on the Prologue and Distinction 37; the Praefatio and Distinctions 1–36 and 38–48 have no interpretations yet, so this does not represent the book as a whole. Within that subset, the Prologue sets out Durandus's account of theology as a plurality of habits—assent to Scripture (identical with faith), defensive/declarative theology, and deduction from the articles—none of which is a science properly so called since the articles are indemonstrable to wayfarers; scriptural theology has the meritorious act as subject and is practical, while defensive theology concerns God as Saviour and is speculative, and theology is neither subalternated to the science of the blessed or to metaphysics. Distinction 37 treats presence in place: God is in all things as their immediate conserving cause and everywhere by filling places with his effects, and angels are present to bodies by order rather than by situs, so that they are not locally moved as subjects.
claims: (Within the covered subset) theology is a cluster of habits, scientific only in a broad sense, oriented chiefly to meritorious action
(Within the covered subset) God is present in all things as their immediate conserving cause and everywhere by repletion
(Within the covered subset) angels are present to bodies by order rather than by spatial situs

jsnvu6-d1e2303.summary: Partial summary of Book II, resting only on Distinction 44, the book's final distinction; the Praefatio and Distinctions 1–43 have no interpretations yet, so this says nothing about the book's treatment of creation, angels, human nature, grace, and sin. Within that subset, Book II closes with a treatment of power and obedience: all power, including the power to sin, is from God; prelacy is divinely instituted by right reason though its abuse is not, and servile domination arose only after sin; Christians owe conscientious obedience to secular rulers, even unbelieving ones, within their legitimate scope; and religious obedience is bounded by the vow and the rule, with papal authority supreme in the Church yet limited to edification and genuine ecclesial utility.
claims: (Within the covered subset) all power, including the power to sin, is from God
(Within the covered subset) obedience to secular and ecclesiastical superiors is owed within the scope of their legitimate authority, and unqualified obedience only to God

jsnvu6.summary: Partial summary of Durandus of Saint-Pourçain's Commentary on the Sentences (Redactio C), resting only on the partial Book I entry (Prologue and Distinction 37) and the partial Book II entry (Distinction 44); the remaining distinctions of Books I and II and all of Books III and IV are not yet interpreted, so this is not a summary of the whole work. Within that subset, the commentary shows Durandus's characteristic positions: a deflationary account of theology as several habits that are scientific only in a broad sense, centred on Scripture and the meritorious act, with God as subject only under the ratio of Saviour; an analysis of divine and angelic presence by 'order' rather than spatial situs; and, at the close of Book II, an account of power and obedience in which all power derives from God while obedience to secular, religious, and papal superiors is bounded by the legitimate scope of their authority.
claims: (Within the covered subset) theology is not a science properly so called but a cluster of habits oriented chiefly to meritorious action
(Within the covered subset) divine and angelic presence are explained by order rather than spatial situs
(Within the covered subset) obedience to any human authority, including the pope, is bounded by the legitimate scope of that authority
